bibliography.abstract: Abstract This article asks how place is produced in the spatial experience of blind people. It works from a phenomenological understanding of place as a densification of embodied experience, developed in the register of critical phenomenology and attentive to the unequal conditions under which different bodies dwell, and elaborates a distinction between two modes in which place is produced. Geometry names the mode in which experience sediments into forms whose contours the body can traverse, repeat and anticipate. Abstraction names the mode in which place takes form without acquiring a contour, orienting through landmarks, atmospheres and networks of belonging that are never delimited. The two are not types of person, not types of place, and not an exhaustive account of how place is made. The argument follows three blind adults, one with congenital and two with acquired blindness, whose lives cross several municipalities in the state of São Paulo, Brazil. Material was generated over two years of fieldwork in Presidente Prudente, a medium-sized city in the west of the state, combining life-history and semi-structured interviews with weekly accompanied journeys. The analysis shows that the two modes do not covary, and that this explains something existing accounts leave joined: autonomy of movement and depth of belonging are separable achievements, produced by different work and obstructed by different features of the city. The article closes by identifying a condition neither mode captures, that of being admitted to a place at all.
bibliography.title: Place through geometry and abstraction: the spatial experience of blind people in a medium-sized Brazilian city

en.caveats: The conceptual framework relies on the experiences of only three individuals in a single regional Brazilian context.
en.what: Through two years of fieldwork in Presidente Prudente, Brazil, incorporating life histories, semi-structured interviews, and weekly accompanied journeys with three blind adults, this study establishes two conceptual modes of place-making: geometry (traversable, predictable spatial forms) and abstraction (orientation via non-delimited landmarks and atmospheres).
en.why: It demonstrates that spatial autonomy and sense of belonging operate independently, showing that urban barriers can disrupt physical mobility without diminishing deep spatial attachment.
